label: Distributional Problems
notes: Chapter 04 turns the modeling languages of earlier chapters into concrete distribution theory. We ask what laws govern the orientation matrix and the latent roots of a sample sum on the Stiefel and Grassmann manifolds, and why those two objects together summarize everything the data say about concentration and direction.

label: The Sample Sum Matrix
notes: Each observation is a frame on the Stiefel manifold; summing the sample produces an unconstrained matrix whose singular value decomposition splits cleanly. The orthogonal factors record orientation while the diagonal of singular values records strength. This factorization is the spine of every distributional result in Chapter 04.

label: Polar Coordinates on Matrices
notes: Writing the sample sum in polar form separates a point on the Stiefel manifold from a positive matrix of latent roots. The Jacobian of this change of variables carries a product of root differences, the same repulsion factor that will later shape the latent-root density and forbid coincident singular values.

label: Matrix Langevin Model
notes: The matrix Langevin density weights a frame by the trace of the parameter matrix against it, so the singular values of that parameter set the concentration. Large singular values pin orientation near a modal frame; small ones flatten the density toward the uniform law on the manifold, giving us a tunable dial.

label: Bingham Model
notes: The Bingham family weights a frame quadratically, through the trace of a symmetric form sandwiched by the frame and its transpose. Because the weight is even, the model is antipodally symmetric and lives naturally on the Grassmann manifold, describing axial data where a direction and its negative are indistinguishable.

label: Orientation and Latent Roots
notes: The decomposition assigns two jobs: the orthogonal factors answer where the data point, and the latent roots answer how tightly they cluster. Inference on direction and inference on concentration become separate questions, and the joint density factors in a way that mirrors that separation almost exactly.

label: Integrating Out the Orientation
notes: To isolate concentration we average the joint density over the orthogonal group, integrating away the orientation factors. The integral over O(m) is not elementary; it produces a hypergeometric function of matrix argument whose two matrix parameters are the concentration matrix and the latent roots themselves.

label: Zonal Polynomials
notes: Zonal polynomials are symmetric functions indexed by partitions that diagonalize integration over the orthogonal group. They are the matrix analogue of power symmetric functions, and every group integral in this chapter expands as a series in zonal polynomials, turning intractable integrals into bookkeeping over partitions.

label: Hypergeometric Functions of Matrix Argument
notes: Collecting zonal polynomial terms with Pochhammer coefficients defines hypergeometric functions of matrix argument. The normalizing constants of the Langevin and Bingham models, and the marginal latent-root densities, are all special cases. These series are the closed-form language Chapter 04 uses for otherwise unevaluable manifold integrals.

label: Latent-Root Density
notes: After integrating out orientation, the latent roots follow a density built from the repulsion factor, an exponential or hypergeometric weight, and the group constant. The repulsion factor pushes roots apart, while concentration pulls the largest root up, so the spread of the spectrum directly reports how organized the sample is.

label: Low versus High Concentration
notes: Under low concentration the latent roots bunch near a diffuse band and orientation is nearly uniform; under high concentration the leading root separates sharply and the modal frame dominates. Comparing the two spectra gives an immediate visual diagnostic for how strongly a manifold sample is structured.

label: Marginal and Conditional Laws
notes: Marginal laws come from integrating one factor away; conditional laws fix it and study the rest. Conditioning on the latent roots leaves an orientation distribution on the Stiefel manifold, while marginalizing over orientation leaves the latent-root law. The two routes answer complementary inferential questions about the same sample.

label: Asymptotics and Approximation
notes: For large concentration the latent-root integrals concentrate near their mode, so Laplace-type expansions and leading zonal terms give accurate approximations. These asymptotics convert the exact hypergeometric series into usable tail estimates and normalizing constants, the practical payoff that makes the distribution theory of Chapter 04 testable.

label: Synthesis
notes: Chapter 04 ties the thread together: decompose the sample sum, model orientation by Langevin or Bingham, integrate out the orthogonal group with zonal polynomials, and read concentration from the latent-root spectrum. Orientation and latent roots are the dual coordinates through which every distributional problem on these manifolds is answered.
